title: NanoQuant: Efficient Sub-1-Bit Quantization of Large Language Models
claim: Our method reaches sub-1-bit storage while staying competitive in quality with baselines that need several times more bits per weight.
layout: 5 panels in a row, one per model, shared legend below
description: Five side-by-side scatter-and-line plots, one for each model: Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3-8B and Rnj-1. The x-axis is bits per weight, from 0 to 5. The y-axis is WikiText2 perplexity on a log scale, from about 5 to 100. A green shaded region with a dashed vertical line at 1 bit is labeled 'Sub-1-Bit' in the first panel. NanoQuant is a bold blue line with circles and sits inside the green region, at low perplexity. The baselines are ARBLLM (purple pentagon), BiLLM (red diamond), GPTQ g64 (orange circles on a dashed line), HBLLM (green square) and STBLLM (magenta triangles). These sit at 2–4+ bits, and several have much higher perplexity. A gray dotted horizontal line marks FP16 perplexity. The eye goes first to the blue NanoQuant curve at the far left. A shared legend runs along the bottom.
caption: Perplexity comparison on WikiText-2. \name reaches 1-bit and sub-1-bit effective storage while remaining competitive with existing binary PTQ baselines that require substantially higher effective BPW.
abstract: Weight-only quantization has become a standard approach for efficiently serving large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods fail to efficiently compress models to binary (1-bit) levels, as they either require large amounts of data and compute or incur additional storage. In this work, we propose NanoQuant, the first post-training quantization (PTQ) method to compress LLMs to both binary and sub-1-bit levels. NanoQuant formulates quantization as a low-rank binary factorization problem, and compresses full-precision weights to low-rank binary matrices and scales. Specifically, it utilizes an efficient alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver to precisely initialize latent binary matrices and scales, and then tunes the initialized parameters through a block and model reconstruction process. Consequently, NanoQuant establishes a new Pareto frontier in low-memory post-training quantization, and enables sub-1-bit compression. NanoQuant makes large-scale deployment feasible on consumer hardware. For example, it compresses Llama2-70B by 25.8$\times$ in just 13 hours on a single H100, enabling a 70B model to operate on a consumer 8 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/SamsungLabs/NanoQuant.
